cards.b: Pathogen: a disease-causing organism. Transmissible disease: one in which the pathogen can be passed from one host to another.
Direct: contact, including blood and body fluids. Indirect: contaminated surfaces, food, animals, air.
A protein coat surrounding genetic material. Viruses are not cells.
Skin, hairs in the nose, mucus, stomach acid and white blood cells.

cards.f: How do control measures reduce disease spread?
cards.b: Clean water, hygienic food preparation, personal hygiene, waste disposal and sewage treatment all stop pathogens being passed on.
A molecule on a pathogen's surface with a specific shape. Each pathogen has its own antigens.
A protein that binds to an antigen, destroying the pathogen directly or marking it for destruction by phagocytes.
It has a shape complementary to one antigen, so it only fits that antigen.
Lymphocytes (a type of white blood cell).
Defence against a pathogen by antibody production in the body. Gained after infection or by vaccination.
Weakened pathogens or antigens are given; antigens stimulate lymphocytes to make antibodies; memory cells give long-term immunity.
On re-infection they cause a faster response with more antibodies, destroying the pathogen before illness.

cards.f: How does vaccinating many people control disease spread?
cards.b: Vaccinated people do not become ill or pass it on, so the pathogen has few hosts and cases fall.
Any substance taken into the body that modifies or affects chemical reactions in the body.
Antibiotics kill non-resistant bacteria; resistant ones survive and reproduce, passing on resistance. Use antibiotics only when essential.

gaps.s: A disease-causing organism is called a ___ .
Antibiotics kill bacteria but do not affect ___ .
Vaccination produces ___ cells that give long-term immunity.
Cells that engulf pathogens by phagocytosis are called ___ .
Stomach acid kills pathogens because it contains ___ acid.
An antibiotic-resistant strain of bacteria is called ___ .
The sticky substance in the airways that traps pathogens is ___ .

short.q: State two ways in which the body prevents pathogens from entering. [2]
short.model: The skin forms a barrier, and mucus and hairs in the nose trap pathogens in inhaled air.
points: mucus / nose hairs trap pathogens (or stomach acid)

short.q: Explain why antibiotics are not used to treat influenza. [2]
short.model: Influenza is caused by a virus, and antibiotics kill bacteria but do not affect viruses.
points: influenza is caused by a virus

short.q: Describe how vaccination gives long-term immunity. [3]
short.model: Weakened pathogens or antigens stimulate lymphocytes to make antibodies, and memory cells are produced that respond quickly if the pathogen returns.
points: weakened pathogen / antigens put into body

short.q: Explain why using antibiotics only when essential limits the development of MRSA. [3]
short.model: Each use of antibiotics selects for resistant bacteria, which survive and reproduce. Less use means fewer chances to select them, so resistance spreads more slowly.
points: resistant bacteria survive antibiotics and reproduce
less use gives less selection / slower spread

short.q: Explain why a specific antibody will not work against a different pathogen. [2]
short.model: Each antibody has a shape complementary to one antigen, and a different pathogen has antigens of a different shape.
points: antibody shape is complementary to a specific antigen
other pathogen's antigens have a different shape so do not fit
